item.title: Unconditional Quantum PAC Learning Advantage in the Large Error Regime
item.description: arXiv:2610.23268v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish an unconditional super-polynomial separation between quantum and classical PAC learning of Boolean functions under the uniform distribution in the large error regime. For every advantage $\lambda(n) = n^{-\omega(1)}$, we construct a concept class that a polynomial-time quantum learner learns to agreement $1/2+\lambda(n)$ with success probability at least $1-1/n^k$. The learner uses only quantum random examples and outputs a polynomial-size deterministic classical circuit. In contrast, no polynomial-time classical learner achieves agreement $1/2 + \lambda(n)/n^k$ with success probability greater than $1/n^k$, even with membership queries. To achieve this, we develop a nearly-optimal quantum learner that uses quantum random examples to produce a hypothesis achieving a prescribed correlation with an arbitrary Boolean function. The learner generalizes Fourier sampling from parity hypotheses to quadratic hypotheses. While standard Fourier sampling is insensitive to the sign of the correlation, we use interference to bias sampling toward positively correlated hypotheses. This is combined with a careful analysis of the resulting distribution to boost both the learner's success probability and its agreement with the target function. We believe that the resulting quantum learning algorithm might be of independent interest. Finally, although a robust quantum PAC learning advantage holds unconditionally in the large error regime, we note that an analogous separation between quantum and classical learning in the small error regime would imply that $\mathsf{NP} \nsubseteq \mathsf{BPP}$.
item.dc:creator: Igor C. Oliveira

item.title: Complexity of liveness in ring Petri nets and of halting in chip-firing on simple digraphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.23523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A ring Petri net (weighted circuit, cyclic weighted T-system) consists of a single directed circuit with arbitrary positive arc weights. We show that deciding liveness of ring Petri nets is coNP-complete, and that coNP-hardness holds in the strong sense already for token-conserving rings, in which every transition consumes and produces the same number of tokens. The proof is a short reduction from the covering problem for systems of residue classes (the complement of Simultaneous Incongruences). Together with a known reduction to circuits, it follows that liveness of weighted T-systems (weighted marked graphs, synchronous dataflow graphs) is coNP-complete, and coNP-hard in the strong sense. As a further consequence, the halting problem for chip-firing on simple directed graphs is NP-complete, which answers a question of Farrell and Levine. On 7 October 2026, the problem of liveness was posed to the AI model Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), which found the reduction, also suggesting the application to the chip-firing problem, and wrote a first version of this paper; the human authors checked it and, together with the model, revised it iteratively into the present form.
item.dc:creator: Eike Best, Raymond Devillers, Petr Jan\v{c}ar, Mat\v{e}j O\v{s}\v{t}\'{a}dal

item.title: Puzznic is PSPACE-Complete
item.description: arXiv:2610.23639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that deciding solvability of Puzznic, a falling-block puzzle game originally developed by Taito, is PSPACE-complete. To show hardness we construct a self-closing door gadget using Puzznic's game mechanics. For membership, we show that the configuration space is exponentially bounded and apply Savitch's theorem. We also improve an existing NP-completeness proof for a simpler version of the game known as Cubic, showing that this game is NP-complete even when restricted to only two kinds of blocks.
item.dc:creator: Jake Anderson, Lars Magnus Hvattum, Andr\'as Z. Salamon

item.title: On the Complexity of Symmetric Boolean Functions in Multiparty Private Simultaneous Messages
item.description: arXiv:2610.21216v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multiparty Private Simultaneous Messages (PSM), also known as Decomposable Randomized Encoding (DRE) or information-theoretic garbling, is a model for non-interactive secure computation. Each party encodes its input using shared randomness and sends a message to an evaluator who does not know that randomness. The evaluator must recover the function output without learning anything else about the inputs. Perfect privacy requires identical transcript distributions on inputs with the same output. We also study the weaker notion of support privacy, which requires only that these distributions have the same support. We study the communication complexity of symmetric Boolean functions when each of the $n$ parties holds one input bit. Lower bounds. We prove a superlinear lower bound for support-private PSM protocols computing $OR_n$. Our technique gives $\Omega(n\log n)$ lower bounds for $MAJ_n$ and $EMAJ_n$ (with even $n$), and an $\Omega(n\log q)$ lower bound for $MOD_q$ when $q\leq(1-c)n$ for a fixed constant $c>0$. Upper bounds. We construct perfectly private PSM protocols of total communication $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ for every symmetric Boolean function, improving on the known quadratic bound. For $MAJ_n$, known branching-program constructions yield an upper bound of $O(n\log^3 n\log\log n)$. For $EMAJ_n$ and $MOD_q$ with prime $q$, the lower bounds are tight up to constant factors in the stated regimes. Under support privacy, we obtain $\widetilde{O}(n)$ communication for every symmetric Boolean function. Earlier lower-bound techniques of Ball et al. (ITCS 2020) yield only trivial linear bounds for symmetric Boolean functions. Concurrent and independent work by Holmgren and Wu proves a $\omega(n)$ lower bound for $OR_n$ using the same combinatorial core. Both works used AI assistance.
item.dc:creator: Marshall Ball, Peter Crawford-Kahrl, Vladimir Podolskii, Morgan Prior

item.title: Concrete Functions in Private Simultaneous Quantum Messages: Quantum Advantages and Structural Limitations
item.description: arXiv:2610.23090v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Private simultaneous quantum messages (PSQM) provide a minimal model of noninteractive secure multiparty quantum computation, yet their communication complexity for concrete functions remains poorly understood. We show that familiar total functions already exhibit both genuine quantum advantages and strong structural limitations. For three-party equality on $n$-bit inputs, which determines whether the players' $n$-bit strings are identical, we construct an entanglement-assisted protocol with asymptotic communication $(1.633\ldots)n$ qubits, whereas every perfectly correct protocol without prior entanglement requires at least $3n$ qubits. For three-bit majority, one shared GHZ state and one transmitted qubit per player suffice for perfect correctness and perfect privacy, reducing the communication from the optimal classical cost of six bits to three qubits. Three-bit AND behaves differently. No perfectly correct and perfectly private protocol exists when the players share an arbitrary three-qubit state, apply arbitrary local unitary encodings, and transmit one qubit each. However, increasing the local dimension overcomes this obstruction: one shared three-qutrit GHZ state and one transmitted qutrit per player yield a one-shot protocol with total communication $3\log_2 3$. Together with the six-bit classical lower bound, this gives a strict quantum communication advantage. More generally, for every $k\geq 3$, we construct a perfectly correct and perfectly private one-shot protocol for $k$-bit AND using one qudit of dimension at most $k$ per player, and hence at most $k\log_2 k$ qubits in total.
item.dc:creator: Harumichi Nishimura

item.title: The Strong Total Cover Problem
item.description: arXiv:2610.23312v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Strong Total Cover Problem (STCP) is a novel covering problem defined on a graph $G = (V, E)$, where the objective is to find a minimum-cardinality subset $T \subseteq V \cup E$ such that every element of $V \cup E$ is covered. In this setting, a vertex covers itself and all its incident edges, while an edge covers itself together with its two endpoints. The STCP resembles classical covering problems such as Vertex Cover and Edge Cover problems, and naturally arises as the dual of the total matching problem. In this paper, we investigate the STCP from algorithmic, complexity, and polyhedral perspectives. We first establish close connections between STCP, the Dominating Set Problem, and the Maximum Induced Matching Problem. These relationships provide structural insights, imply the NP-hardness of STCP, and identify graph classes for which the problem is polynomial-time solvable. We then investigate the weighted version of STCP, showing that it remains NP-hard even on complete graphs with binary weights. On the other hand, we present a 2-approximation algorithm, and a polynomial-time algorithm for complete bipartite graphs. On the polyhedral side, we introduce the Strong Total Cover Polytope and derive several families of valid inequalities, some of which are shown to define facets. Finally, we provide a complete linear description of the associated polytope for triangular cactus graphs, revealing an interesting contrast with the considerably more intricate facial structure of the dominating set polytope on cactus graphs.
item.dc:creator: Manuel Aprile, Luca Ferrarini

item.title: Electrostatic Limits on Quantum Spatial Search
item.description: arXiv:2610.23560v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove that a quantum walker cannot search a two-dimensional lattice in Grover's $O(\sqrt N)$ time, resolving the long-standing open question posed by Aaronson and Ambainis in 2003. A walker that hops between neighbouring sites of an $L\times L$ lattice, $N=L^2$, needs $\Omega(\sqrt{N\log N})$ local steps at least to find a marked vertex, even with unlimited memory and free queries. Hence, Tulsi's algorithm is asymptotically optimal. Our proof rests on a surprising correspondence with classical electrostatics. We treat the marked vertex as a point charge and weight the overlap between the walker's states with and without the mark by the potential drop, which vanishes where queries act. Only local steps change this weighted overlap, at a rate limited by the field energy, so the lower bound is set by the self-potential of the charge. In the plane this self-potential grows logarithmically with system size, like the Coulomb potential, leading to the extra root-logarithmic factor. Several marked vertices turn the charge into a conductor, and the lower bound depends on their arrangement through its capacitance.
item.dc:creator: Weikang Li

item.title: Exponentially Fewer-Server PIR from Sparser $S$-Decoding Polynomials
item.description: arXiv:2607.22033v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that under a plausible number-theoretic conjecture, for any constant $s$ there exists an $s$-server private information retrieval (PIR) protocol that on an $n$-bit database requires communication $\exp(O((\log n)^{1/s} (\log \log n)^{1-1/s}))$. This achieves a superpolynomial improvement in communication when $s \geq 4$; previous constructions attaining the same communication required $2^{O(s)}$ servers. Our number-theoretic conjecture is implied by existing conjectures, namely the generalized repunit conjecture and Schinzel's hypothesis H (either one of these conjectures would suffice alone). Our result builds on the "matching vector family + $S$-decoding polynomials" framework pioneered by Efremenko (STOC 2009) and recently refined by Ghasemi, Kopparty, and Sudan (STOC 2025). The main ingredient is a framework for constructing $S$-decoding polynomials with only $k+1$ nonzero coefficients modulo special products of $k$ primes, resolving an open problem posed by Ghasemi and Kopparty (ITCS 2026). By the lower bound shown by Ghasemi and Kopparty, this is the minimum achievable sparsity. We also empirically validate our construction and make our result unconditional for all $s \leq 15$. We also apply our techniques to regimes where $s$ grows with $n$, showing under a stronger variant of our number-theoretic conjecture that the communication complexity of $s$-server matching-vector PIR can be superpolynomially reduced from the previous state of the art for any $s \leq \exp(o(\sqrt{\log \log n/\log \log \log n}))$. The main result for $s = O(1)$ and its proof were discovered in a GPT-5.5 Pro conversation prompted by the authors.
item.dc:creator: Aparna Gupte, Seyoon Ragavan

item.title: Metric Dimension is NP-complete on Graphs of Treewidth Two
item.description: arXiv:2610.21133v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The metric dimension of a connected graph is the least number of vertices whose distance vectors distinguish all vertices. We show that deciding whether the metric dimension of a graph is at most a given integer is NP-complete on graphs of treewidth at most two. As the problem is polynomial on trees, the graphs of treewidth one, this settles the treewidth threshold of its hardness, which was known to lie between two and twenty-four. The reduction is from satisfiability of formulas in which every literal occurs at most twice. To such a formula with $n$ clauses and $r$ variables it associates a graph $G_\varphi$ of treewidth at most two with $O((n+r)^2)$ vertices, whose metric dimension is $2(n+r)+5$ if the formula is satisfiable and $2(n+r)+6$ otherwise.
item.dc:creator: Tristan Benoit

item.title: MIP*=RE
item.description: arXiv:2001.04383v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show that the class MIP* of languages that can be decided by a classical verifier interacting with multiple all-powerful quantum provers sharing entanglement is equal to the class RE of recursively enumerable languages. Our proof builds upon the quantum low-degree test of (Natarajan and Vidick, FOCS 2018) and the classical low-individual degree test of (Ji, et al., 2020) by integrating recent developments from (Natarajan and Wright, FOCS 2019) and combining them with the recursive compression framework of (Fitzsimons et al., STOC 2019). An immediate byproduct of our result is that there is an efficient reduction from the Halting Problem to the problem of deciding whether a two-player nonlocal game has entangled value $1$ or at most $1/2$. Using a known connection, undecidability of the entangled value implies a negative answer to Tsirelson's problem: we show, by providing an explicit example, that the closure $C_{qa}$ of the set of quantum tensor product correlations is strictly included in the set $C_{qc}$ of quantum commuting correlations. Following work of (Fritz, Rev. Math. Phys. 2012) and (Junge et al., J. Math. Phys. 2011) our results provide a refutation of Connes' embedding conjecture from the theory of von Neumann algebras.
item.dc:creator: Zhengfeng Ji, Anand Natarajan, Thomas Vidick, John Wright, Henry Yuen

item.title: Recognizing 2-Layer and Outer $k$-Planar Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2412.04042v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The crossing number of a graph is the least number of crossings over all drawings of the graph in the plane. Computing the crossing number of a given graph is NP-hard, but fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) with respect to the natural parameter. Two well-known variants of the problem are 2-layer crossing minimization and circular crossing minimization, where every vertex must lie on one of two layers, namely two parallel lines, or a circle, respectively. Both variants are NP-hard, but FPT with respect to the natural parameter. Recently, a local version of the crossing number has also received considerable attention. A graph is $k$-planar if it admits a drawing with at most $k$ crossings per edge. In contrast to the crossing number, recognizing $k$-planar graphs is NP-hard even if $k=1$. In this paper, we consider the two above variants in the local setting. The $k$-planar graphs that admit a straight-line drawing with vertices on two layers or on a circle are called 2-layer $k$-planar and outer $k$-planar graphs, respectively. We study the parameterized complexity of the two recognition problems with respect to $k$. For $k=0$, both problems can easily be solved in linear time. Two groups independently showed that outer 1-planar graphs can also be recognized in linear time [Hong et al., Algorithmica 2015; Auer et al., Algorithmica 2016]. One group asked whether outer 2-planar graphs can be recognized in polynomial time. Our main contribution consists of XP-algorithms for recognizing 2-layer $k$-planar graphs and outer $k$-planar graphs. We complement these results by showing that both recognition problems are XNLP-hard. This implies that both problems are W$[t]$-hard for every $t$ and that it is unlikely that they admit FPT-algorithms. On the other hand, we present an FPT-algorithm for recognizing 2-layer $k$-planar graphs where the order of the vertices on one layer is specified.
item.dc:creator: Yasuaki Kobayashi, Yuto Okada, Alexander Wolff

item.title: Sparse Polynomial GCD Cannot Be Computed in Fixed-output Polynomial Time
item.description: arXiv:2606.12144v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper shows that, assuming $\mathsf{P}\ne\mathsf{NP}$, sparse univariate polynomial GCD cannot be computed in fixed-output polynomial time over any fixed computable field. Precisely, there is no deterministic algorithm that can compute the GCD of sparse univariate polynomials over any fixed computable field with total bit complexity polynomial in the input size, with the output size as a fixed parameter. In particular, there is no deterministic algorithm for sparse polynomial GCD that runs in polynomial time with respect to both the input and the output sizes. This settles the open problem posed as Challenge 5 in the sparsity challenges. Furthermore, we show that the Roots of Unity Detection problem over finite fields is NP-hard under random reductions; that is, determining whether the GCD of a sparse univariate polynomial and $x^n - 1$ has nonzero degree is NP-hard.
item.dc:creator: Yichuan Cao, Ruyong Feng, Xiao-Shan Gao, Qiao-Long Huang, Ruichen Qiu

item.title: Vanilla Exact Synthesis of CNOT Circuits is NP-hard
item.description: arXiv:2609.04160v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Exact CNOT synthesis seeks a minimum-size circuit implementing a given invertible binary linear transformation. We study its vanilla formulation: synthesis from the identity on fixed labeled qubits, without ancillas and with all-to-all connectivity. We prove that this problem is NP-hard and that its bounded decision version is NP-complete. Hardness persists even for unitriangular targets that are low-rank perturbations of the identity and under near-linear gate budgets. Our proof gives a polynomial-time reduction from the NP-complete Hamiltonian path problem on grid graphs. A unary hypercube embedding translates graph vertices into circuit parities and edge traversals into CNOT updates. The central challenge is that Hamiltonian paths require intermediate vertex visits, whereas exact synthesis constrains only the final transformation. We bridge this gap with a replicated recorder qubits construction that encodes the required parities in the final outputs, together with a tight gate budget that forces every sufficiently short implementation to trace a Hamiltonian path. Crucially, this path structure is enforced by the construction rather than imposed as a restriction on the circuit. The result directly implies NP-hardness for shortest word problem and Cayley-graph distance computation over $\mathrm{GL}(n,2)$ with elementary transvections as generators, as well as fixed-width sequential XOR program minimization. For CNOT-minimal exact phase polynomial synthesis, it yields NP-hardness with a zero phase polynomial; extending the reduction to grid-graph Hamiltonian cycle problem establishes hardness even when the final linear transformation is the identity. These complementary results show that the linear and phase components each independently suffice for NP-hardness of exact phase polynomial synthesis.
item.dc:creator: Chenjian Li, Ji Guan

item.title: A deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for the Bilu--Linial signing problem on bipartite graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.09972v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for the Bilu--Linial signing problem on bipartite graphs. For every finite simple bipartite graph of maximum degree at most an integer $\Delta\ge3$, the algorithm assigns signs to its edges so that the signed adjacency matrix has operator norm strictly less than $2\sqrt{\Delta-1}$. Our algorithm builds on the randomized recursive repair framework of Jadbabaie, Saberi, and Sra~\cite{JSS26}, with deterministic rules for sign selection and vertex deletion.
item.dc:creator: Zhiqiang Xu
